The story achieves an appropriate and effective balance between scene and summary/exposition. The narrative unfolds primarily in real-time through vivid, atmospheric scenes—the starting of the ferry's engine, the brief dialogues with the baker's son, the old man, and the out-of-place woman with the suitcase, as well as the tense final moment with the ringing telephone. Woven seamlessly into these four-minute river crossings are concise moments of summary and exposition that never bog down the pacing. Instead, the exposition provides essential context that deepens the scenes: we learn Ilse has been doing this for thirty-five years, we understand the familiar routines of the locals (like Pommerening going to the barber despite having no hair), and, most importantly, we get brief background on Jonas in Munich, which gives the final scene with the ringing phone its emotional weight.
